newsitem.title: USA: Chicago's Cardinal Bernardin reported near death.
newsitem.headline: Chicago's Cardinal Bernardin reported near death.

text.p: Cardinal Joseph Bernardin, who has battled cancer for more than a year, was in grave condition on Wednesday, the Archdiocese of Chicago said.
The 68-year-old prelate, senior cardinal in the church's U.S. hierarchy, was confined to bed at his home and has not appeared in public in recent days.
"The cardinal's condition is grave," said Mary McDonough, spokeswoman for the archdiocese. She said Bernardin received telephone calls from both President Bill Clinton and Pope John Paul.
She said Bernardin spoke directly to Clinton.
The Pope called at mid-afternoon and "gave the cardinal his blessing. He thanked him for all that he had done for the Archdiocese of Chicago and for the universal church," the spokeswoman said.

In June 1995 Bernardin was found to be suffering from pancreatic cancer, a particularly deadly form of the disease, and underwent surgery. Last August 30 he announced the disease had spread to his liver and was inoperable, giving him less than a year to live.
A few weeks ago he abandoned chemotherapy treatments.
Bernardin is the longest-serving active U.S. cardinal, appointed by Pope John Paul in 1982 to head the 2.3 million-member Chicago archdiocese, the nation's second-largest after Los Angeles.

Hundreds of delegates to the National Conference of Catholic Bishops in Washington stood and applauded in solidarity on Wednesday with the gravely ill Bernardin, after a letter that he wrote to the Supreme Court opposing a right to assisted suicide was read out.

"I am at the end of my earthly life," Bernardin said in a November 7 letter to the high court. "I know from my own experience that patients often face difficult and deeply personal decisions about their care. However, I also know that even a person who decides to forego treatment does not necessarily choose death."

He continued: "There can be no such thing as a 'right to assisted suicide' because there can be no legal and moral order which tolerates the killing of innocent human life, even if the agent of death is self-administered."
The American Catholic bishops responded with a long standing ovation and sustained applause after Bishop Anthony Pilla of Cleveland read Bernardin's letter.
